output.summary: A loyalty mobile app (iOS and Android) for 22 bakery shops, with points, rewards, push offers, a QR code scanned at the till and a back office for campaigns. It closely resembles a past coffee-chain project (35 stores, paper stamp card, old registers with no API, anniversary deadline), which took 760 hours. The main technical risk is getting points from the old tills to the backend. Past experience suggests a small agent on each shop computer with an offline retry queue, costed as its own line item. The anniversary deadline is also a risk until a date is confirmed.
open_questions: What is the anniversary campaign date, and is a hard launch date required or is a pilot in a few shops acceptable?
What till models and operating systems are in the 22 shops, and is there a shop computer on which a small agent can be installed?
If the tills cannot be linked to a computer, is cashier-entered or QR-scan-only point capture acceptable?
How reliable is the internet in the affected shops, and can points be credited with a delay after the sale?
How many customers are expected in the first six months?
Who will own the back office day to day (campaigns, redemptions), and how much training do shop staff have?
Are there data residency or privacy requirements (e.g. consent for push offers, account deletion)?
Is cross-platform development acceptable, and do you already have Apple and Google developer accounts?

output.summary: Android app for rugged handheld scanners used by about 40 pickers. It guides each picker along a route, verifies every item by barcode, works offline when wifi drops, and syncs with the client's warehouse management system (WMS) API. This is closely comparable to a past delivered project (b012), a picking app with offline mode and a WMS REST API for 60 pickers, which took 690 hours. Adjusting for a slightly smaller picker count and the unknowns about devices and API, a reasonable range is about 560 to 800 hours.

Is a supervisor screen or productivity reporting required, as it was in the past project?
How are short picks, substitutions and damaged items handled?
What are the pilot and rollout plans and the deadline?
How large are the warehouse and the product catalogue, and which barcode formats are used?
Are there requirements for authentication, picker login and device management?

The analyst workflow goes live first and the applicant portal second. This closely matches one past project (b014, a regional credit cooperative's loan application workflow), which delivered in 1,600 hours and about $155,000 with the same two-phase launch. output.summary: Web streaming subscription site for an educational film publisher: about 600 hours of video with some regional licensing limits, DRM-style content protection, subscription payments with trials and coupons, subtitle management and basic analytics, with a fixed festival launch date. The closest past project is b023, a video subscription site for a documentary library with nearly the same feature set. It took 1,450 hours (estimated 1,000) mainly because of DRM requirements, library conversion and subtitle fixes. The new library is smaller (600 vs 800 hours), so a somewhat lower range is plausible, but DRM level and the state of the content are still unknown. The telemedicine project (b006) is not comparable in scope and is not used for the estimate.
open_questions: What DRM level or content protection do the rights holders require (for example, a specific studio-grade DRM), and is it written in the licence agreements?
Which countries are subject to regional licensing limits, and are they per title or per catalog?
What format and quality is the 600-hour library in, and does it need conversion to streaming formats?
Do subtitles already exist for all content? In which languages, and in what formats?
What is the date of the festival launch, and is a reduced catalog at launch acceptable?
Which payment provider and which currencies and tax rules (VAT) are needed?
What analytics are needed beyond views and churn, and who consumes them?
Is there an existing website, user base or content management system to integrate with?
What expected number of subscribers and concurrent viewers should the video platform be sized for?
Who is responsible for ingesting and tagging the content, the client or us?

output.summary: The client wants a modern, good-looking company website and asks for a cost. The brief gives no information about the company, the site's purpose, the number of pages, the features needed, the content or the timeline. The past projects in the sources are a property listing portal, a video subscription site, a shoe shop migration, an online course platform and a finance app. These are complex, transactional products, not a company website, so none is a valid basis for an estimate. Any figure drawn from them would be false precision, so no estimate is given. A scoping conversation should come first.
open_questions: What does the company do, and what is the main goal of the website (brand presence, lead generation, selling products, recruiting)?
Is this a new site or a redesign of an existing one? If it exists, what is wrong with it?
Roughly how many pages or sections are needed, and in how many languages?
Which features are required (contact forms, blog, CMS, booking, e-commerce, user accounts, integrations)?
Who will provide the content (copy, photos, video, logo and brand guidelines), or is writing and design of those assets in scope?
Are there example websites the client considers modern and good looking?
What is the budget range and the desired launch date?
Who will maintain the site after launch, and are hosting, SEO, analytics and ongoing support in scope?

risks.description: Vague requirements ('modern and good looking') make scope and acceptance criteria subjective, which risks repeated design revisions and budget overruns.

Without knowing whether the site is informational or transactional, the cost could differ by more than an order of magnitude. Past projects of the transactional kind, such as portals and shops, were far larger than a typical company website.
Content, branding and ownership of assets are unspecified, so delays in client-supplied content could hold up the launch.

insufficient_info: The brief does not state the purpose, size, features, content or timeline of the website, so no scope can be defined.

None of the retrieved past projects is a comparable corporate or marketing website. They are a listing portal, a video subscription platform, an e-commerce migration, a course platform and a mobile app, so their actual hours and costs would not give a reliable range.
No budget or deadline is given to calibrate against.

sources.text: A regional media company with a library of documentaries wants to sell monthly subscriptions to stream them online. Currently the content is on DVD and a free video site with low revenue. Management wants to launch in time for a major festival.
sources.title: Video subscription site

sources.text: Passo Certo sells shoes online and in 14 physical stores. Their online shop runs on a custom PHP system written eight years ago by a freelancer who is no longer around. It is slow during sales and nobody dares to change it. They asked us to move the shop to a modern platform without losing their search ranking.
sources.title: Shoe retailer store migration

sources.text: A professional training company teaches certification courses in person to about 5,000 students a year and wants its own online platform. Today they sell their courses on a third-party marketplace and pay high commissions.
sources.title: Online course platform

output.summary: The brief asks for firmware for a satellite ground-station antenna controller. It covers real-time motor control on a custom microcontroller board, radiation-tolerant design reviews and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing. None of the retrieved past projects involve embedded firmware, real-time control, custom hardware, radiation-tolerant design or HIL testing. They are web, mobile, data-pipeline and integration projects. Their hours and costs would not give a defensible estimate for this work, so no estimate is provided. The past projects do offer general lessons that apply here: hardware and legacy-device integration tends to overrun, and compliance or review requirements should be clarified before quoting.
open_questions: Which microcontroller and board is used, and is the board design finished or still changing? Are prototype boards available, and how many?
What are the motor type and control requirements (axes, stepper or servo, control loop rates, pointing accuracy, tracking speed)?
Is an RTOS or bare-metal approach required, and is there existing firmware or a code base to build on?
What does 'radiation-tolerant design reviews' involve? Which standards apply, who performs the reviews, and are we producing documentation or only participating?
Does the ground-station antenna actually need radiation tolerance, and what environment is it deployed in?
What does the HIL setup involve? Does the client already have a test rig, simulators or motor and encoder models, or must we build them?
What interfaces must the controller support (satellite tracking software, network protocols, telemetry, operator UI)?
What safety, limit-switch, fail-safe and certification requirements apply?
What are the delivery timeline, the team composition expected and the acceptance criteria?
Is the estimate for engineering effort only, or does it include hardware, test equipment and certification costs?

risks.description: Integrating with existing or custom hardware that is poorly documented can cause large overruns. A past project lost about 110 hours to unexpected issues with software on the client's old machines, and this brief involves a custom board that may be even less predictable.

citations.quote: any software installed on the client's old store machines needs its own line in the estimate

risks.description: Compliance or review requirements may surface late. Radiation-tolerance reviews could add unplanned work if their scope and acceptance criteria are not agreed before quoting.

citations.quote: ask about compliance reviews and test environments before quoting

risks.description: Test environments may be unavailable or late. HIL testing depends on rigs, simulators and prototype boards, and delays in these would block validation.

risks.description: Real-time motor control and hardware-in-the-loop work require specialist embedded skills and iteration on physical hardware. None of the past projects cover this, so the effort is very uncertain.
The scope of the radiation-tolerant design review is undefined and could grow into redesign work, such as changes to the board, memory protection or watchdog strategy.

sources.text: Delivered in 1,900 hours against an estimate of 1,200, a large overrun. Getting data out of the old controllers took about 500 hours: custom protocol adapters, network approvals and sensors that had to be installed. Without labeled failures we could only build alert rules and simple anomaly detection, not a true failure predictor. The client accepted this after the pilot. Lesson: industrial data projects spend most of the effort on data acquisition, and the machine learning promise must be reduced when there are no labels.
sources.title: Predictive maintenance pipeline

sources.text: Delivered in 1,400 hours against an estimate of 1,100. The three vendor APIs behaved very differently: one had undocumented rate limits, one sent timestamps in local time without a timezone, and one changed its payload format once during the project. Normalizing the data into one model took about 200 hours more than planned. The real-time map was done within the first phase as expected. The fuel report was descoped halfway because one vendor did not expose fuel sensors. The client is happy with the map and the late-delivery alerts. Lesson: budget extra time for every external API, and ask for sample payloads before the estimate.
sources.title: Fleet tracking dashboards

sources.text: A two-person startup wants to launch a personal finance app that connects to users' bank accounts, categorizes spending automatically and gives savings tips. The founders have a design in Figma and some seed money. They contacted us and three other agencies for a quote.
sources.title: Personal finance mobile app

sources.text: Delivered in 760 hours against an estimate of 600. The mobile app was quick. The register agent was the problem: store computers had different Windows versions and flaky internet, and we had to build an offline queue that retried sending points. That alone was around 110 hours not in the estimate. Apple's review rejected the first submission over account deletion, a two-day delay. Lesson: any software installed on the client's old store machines needs its own line in the estimate.
sources.title: Loyalty app for a coffee chain

sources.text: Delivered in 1,100 hours against an estimate of 900. Video itself was easy using a managed video API. The overrun came from the SAML integration (about 90 hours, the insurer's test environment was down for weeks) and from compliance reviews of the prescription flow, which the client only revealed after the first demo. Load tests showed the video provider's free tier was not enough, which changed the monthly cost for the client. Lesson: ask about compliance reviews and test environments before quoting.
sources.title: Telemedicine platform
